claim: The evolution of a mobile neck was a key innovation at the origin of tetrapods.
source: The evolution of a mobile neck was a key innovation at the origin of tetrapods (Daeschler et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daeschler et al., 2006

claim: Cranial muscles are distinct from trunk muscles in genetic regulation and susceptibility to disease.
source: They are distinct from trunk muscles in genetic regulation and susceptibility to disease (Noden, 1983; Noden et al., 1999; Sambasivan et al., 2009; reviewed by Bismuth and Relaix, 2010; Diogo et al., 2015; Noden and Francis-West, 2006; Tzahor, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Cranial muscles arise from cranial paraxial and splanchnic mesoderm, not from somites.
source: Developmentally, they are non-somitic, arising instead from cranial paraxial and splanchnic mesoderm (Couly et al., 1992; Noden, 1983; Evans and Noden, 2006; reviewed by Noden and Trainor, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to developmental studies

claim: Cranial muscle regulatory factors include Isl1, Tbx1, MyoR, Capsulin and Pitx2.
source: Cranial muscle regulatory factors include Isl1, Tbx1, MyoR, Capsulin and Pitx2, which operate in specific muscle groups (Hacker and Guthrie, 1998; Sambasivan et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2002; Mootoosamy and Dietrich, 2002; Harel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to molecular studies

claim: Pitx2 specifies mandibular arch mesoderm but not hyoid arch mesoderm in the mouse.
source: Pitx2, for example, specifies mandibular arch mesoderm but not hyoid arch mesoderm in the mouse (Shih et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shih et al., 2007a

claim: Formation of trunk muscle is Pax3-dependent.
source: In contrast to cranial muscle, formation of trunk muscle is Pax3-dependent (Tajbakhsh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tajbakhsh et al., 1997

claim: Hypobranchial muscles are derived from occipital somites.
source: Hypobranchial muscles are derived from occipital somites, which form the hypoglossal cord and migrate towards the tongue (Noden, 1983; O'Rahilly and Müller, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Noden, 1983 and O'Rahilly and Müller, 1984

claim: The number of occipital somites contributing to cranial structures varies among species.
source: The number of occipital somites contributing to cranial structures varies among species, however.
evidence: Stated as a general observation in the text

claim: In axolotl, somites 2 and 3 form both hypobranchial musculature and the occipital arch.
source: For example, somites 2 and 3 form both hypobranchial musculature and the occipital arch in the axolotl (Piekarski and Olsson, 2007; 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Piekarski and Olsson, 2007 and 2014

claim: In chicken, somites 2–5 form both the occipital region of the skull and tongue musculature.
source: whereas in chicken somites 2–5 form both the occipital region of the skull and tongue musculature (Couly et al., 1993; Huang et al., 1999; 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Couly et al., 1993 and Huang et al., 1999, 2000

claim: The cucullaris muscle is a feature of gnathostomes.
source: The cucullaris muscle, a feature of gnathostomes, connects the head to the pectoral girdle, thus spanning the transition zone between cranial and trunk myogenic signaling regimes (Kuratani, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuratani, 1997

claim: The cucullaris is the putative homologue of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid in amniotes.
source: It is the putative homologue of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid in amniotes (Lubosch et al., 1938).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lubosch et al., 1938

claim: In sharks and the Queensland lungfish, the cucullaris elevates the gill arches and protracts the pectoral girdle.
source: In sharks and the Queensland lungfish, the cucullaris elevates the gill arches and protracts the pectoral girdle.
evidence: Stated as an anatomical observation in the text

claim: The cucullaris originates near the skull and continues caudally and ventrally to insert on the scapular region of the pectoral girdle.
source: It originates near the skull and continues caudally and ventrally to insert on the scapular region of the pectoral girdle; a ventral fascicle extends to the posteriormost branchial bar (Edgeworth, 1926; 1935; Allis, 1917; Vetter, 1874; Greenwood and Lauder, 1981).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies

claim: The cucullaris is innervated by the accessory ramus of the vagus (X) nerve in anamniotes.
source: It is innervated by the accessory ramus of the vagus (X) nerve in anamniotes, but primarily by the accessory (XI) nerve in amniotes (Edgeworth, 1935).
evidence: Supported by citation to Edgeworth, 1935

claim: The cucullaris is innervated primarily by the accessory (XI) nerve in amniotes.
source: It is innervated by the accessory ramus of the vagus (X) nerve in anamniotes, but primarily by the accessory (XI) nerve in amniotes (Edgeworth, 1935).
evidence: Supported by citation to Edgeworth, 1935

claim: In chicken, the connective-tissue component of hypobranchial muscles and the ventrolateral neck region is derived from neural crest.
source: While in chicken the connective-tissue component of hypobranchial muscles and the ventrolateral neck region is derived from neural crest (Le Lièvre and Le Douarin, 1975)
evidence: Supported by citation to Le Lièvre and Le Douarin, 1975

claim: The cucullaris is reported to have somite-derived connective tissue.
source: the cucullaris is reported to have somite-derived connective tissue (Noden, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Noden, 1983

claim: The derivation of connective-tissue components of the mouse trapezius is not fully resolved.
source: The derivation of connective-tissue components of the mouse trapezius is not fully resolved; both lateral plate mesoderm (Durland et al., 2008) and neural crest (Matsuoka et al., 2005) are reported sources.
evidence: Supported by citations to conflicting studies

claim: The cucullaris was historically considered a branchiomeric cranial muscle based in part on its anatomical relation to the gill levators.
source: Historically, the cucullaris was considered a branchiomeric cranial muscle based in part on its anatomical relation to the gill levators (Vetter, 1874; Edgeworth, 1935; Piatt, 1938).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical anatomical studies

claim: Fate mapping of anterior somites in chicken and axolotl demonstrated a somitic (trunk) contribution to the cucullaris.
source: Subsequent fate mapping of anterior somites in chicken and axolotl, though, demonstrated a somitic (trunk) contribution (Noden, 1983; Couly et al., 1993; Huang et al., 1997; 2000; Piekarski and Olsson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to fate-mapping studies

claim: Recent fate mapping in chicken and genetic analysis in mouse reveal that the trapezius is primarily a lateral plate mesoderm-derived structure that employs a cranial myogenic program.
source: More recent fate mapping in chicken and genetic analysis in mouse reveal that the trapezius is primarily a lateral plate mesoderm-derived structure that employs a cranial, rather than trunk, myogenic program (Theis et al., 2010; Lescroart et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Theis et al., 2010 and Lescroart et al., 2015

claim: Axolotls possess bushy external gills and their associated musculature, which likely were present in the larvae of Paleozoic tetrapods.
source: Moreover, axolotls possess bushy external gills and their associated musculature, which likely were present in the larvae of Paleozoic tetrapods
evidence: Inference based on comparative anatomy

claim: Axolotls possess a robust gill skeleton, which was present in the earliest limbed stem tetrapods.
source: as well as a robust gill skeleton, which was present in the earliest limbed stem tetrapods (Schoch and Witzmann, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoch and Witzmann, 2011

claim: Novel computed tomography datasets reveal broad conservation of the cucullaris in gnathostomes, including coelacanth and caecilian.
source: Novel computed tomography datasets reveal broad conservation of the cucullaris in gnathostomes, including coelacanth and caecilian, two sarcopterygians previously thought to lack it.
evidence: Based on CT data presented in the manuscript

claim: Coelacanth and caecilian are two sarcopterygians previously thought to lack the cucullaris.
source: Novel computed tomography datasets reveal broad conservation of the cucullaris in gnathostomes, including coelacanth and caecilian, two sarcopterygians previously thought to lack it.
evidence: Reference to previous understanding in the literature

claim: In chicken, lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) adjacent to occipital somites is a recently identified embryonic source of cervical musculature.
source: In chicken, lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) adjacent to occipital somites is a recently identified embryonic source of cervical musculature.
evidence: Reference to recent findings in the literature

claim: Fate-mapping in axolotl demonstrates that LPM adjacent to occipital somites contributes to posterior gill-levator muscles and the cucullaris.
source: We fate-map this mesoderm in the axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum), which retains external gills, and demonstrate its contribution to posterior gill-levator muscles and the cucullaris.
evidence: Based on fate-mapping experiments presented in the manuscript

claim: LPM adjacent to the occipital somites should be regarded as posterior cranial mesoderm.
source: Accordingly, LPM adjacent to the occipital somites should be regarded as posterior cranial mesoderm.
evidence: Inference drawn from fate-mapping data

claim: The axial position of the head-trunk border in axolotl is congruent between LPM and somitic mesoderm.
source: The axial position of the head-trunk border in axolotl is congruent between LPM and somitic mesoderm, unlike in chicken and possibly other amniotes.
evidence: Based on fate-mapping data presented in the manuscript

claim: The axial position of the head-trunk border in chicken is not congruent between LPM and somitic mesoderm.
source: The axial position of the head-trunk border in axolotl is congruent between LPM and somitic mesoderm, unlike in chicken and possibly other amniotes.
evidence: Comparison with chicken based on literature and data

claim: In chimaera, the cucullaris is a massive muscle that may incorporate anterior gill levators.
source: In Chondrichthyes, such as the chimaera, the cucullaris is a massive muscle that may incorporate anterior gill levators; in this respect, it may not be strictly homologous, in its entirety, with the cucullaris of osteichthyans.
evidence: Based on CT imaging data presented in the manuscript

claim: The cucullaris in chimaera may not be strictly homologous, in its entirety, with the cucullaris of osteichthyans.
source: In Chondrichthyes, such as the chimaera, the cucullaris is a massive muscle that may incorporate anterior gill levators; in this respect, it may not be strictly homologous, in its entirety, with the cucullaris of osteichthyans.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical observations

claim: In piscine osteichthyans, such as bichir and lungfish, the cucullaris is a thin, strap-like muscle.
source: In piscine osteichthyans, such as bichir and lungfish, the cucullaris is a thin, strap-like muscle, sometimes called the 'protractor pectoralis' (e.g., Greenwood and Lauder, 1981).
evidence: Based on CT imaging data and citation to Greenwood and Lauder, 1981

claim: The cucullaris diverges from the anterior gill levators but is in series with them.
source: It diverges from the anterior gill levators, but otherwise it is in series with them, is located in the same connective tissue sheath, and shares muscle fibers with the immediately anterior levators.
evidence: Based on CT imaging observations

claim: The cucullaris originates from the posterior region of the head and inserts on the pectoral girdle and, when present, the fifth gill arch.
source: It originates from the posterior region of the head and inserts on the pectoral girdle and, when present, the fifth gill arch.
evidence: Based on anatomical observations from CT data

claim: In some amphibians and in amniotes, the cucullaris is a large wedge-shaped muscle, sometimes termed the trapezius.
source: In some amphibians and in amniotes, the cucullaris is a large wedge-shaped muscle, sometimes termed the trapezius (Owen, 1866; Edgeworth, 1935; Gegenbaur et al., 1878).
evidence: Based on CT imaging and citations to historical anatomical studies

claim: The cucullaris has not been described in the musculoskeletally conservative coelacanth.
source: The cucullaris has not been described in the musculoskeletally conservative coelacanth, nor in the limbless caecilian amphibians.
evidence: Reference to previous literature

claim: Greenwood and Lauder (1981) reported the cucullaris absent from the coelacanth based on novel dissections.
source: Based on novel dissections, Greenwood and Lauder (1981) reported the cucullaris absent from the coelacanth.
evidence: Citation to Greenwood and Lauder, 1981

claim: Millot and Anthony (1958) described in the coelacanth a fifth gill levator that originates on the anocleithrum of the pectoral girdle.
source: Millot and Anthony (1958), however, had earlier briefly described in the coelacanth a fifth gill levator that originates on the anocleithrum of the pectoral girdle, unlike the first four gill levators, which originate in the otic region.
evidence: Citation to Millot and Anthony, 1958

claim: The fifth gill levator in coelacanth is larger than previously described, with several heads originating on the pectoral girdle.
source: We examined this muscle in both a CT scan of a contrast-stained coelacanth pup and an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scan of an adult. The muscle in these specimens is larger than previously described, with several heads originating on the pectoral girdle (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on CT and MRI imaging data presented in the manuscript

claim: In the adult coelacanth, an anterior portion of the fifth gill levator extends dorsally to attach on the fascia of the epaxial musculature.
source: In the adult, an anterior portion of this muscle extends dorsally to attach on the fascia of the epaxial musculature (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Based on MRI imaging data

claim: The fifth gill levator in coelacanth is the homolog of the cucullaris.
source: Based on its morphology and location, we regard the fifth gill levator as the homolog of the cucullaris.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical observations from imaging data

claim: The coelacanth cucullaris retains the ancestral connection between the posteriormost branchial bar and the pectoral girdle.
source: Accordingly, the coelacanth cucullaris retains the ancestral connection between the posteriormost branchial bar and the pectoral girdle, which is seen in at least some sharks and lungfish (Edgeworth, 1926; 1935; Allis, 1917; Vetter, 1874; Greenwood and Lauder, 1981).
evidence: Inference based on comparative anatomy and citations

claim: In actinopterygians, the cucullaris sometimes joins the fibers of the posteriormost gill levator even though they lack an ossified fifth gill arch.
source: Even though actinopterygians lack an ossified fifth gill arch, the cucullaris in these taxa sometimes joins the fibers of the posteriormost gill levator (Greenwood and Lauder, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greenwood and Lauder, 1981

claim: In the caecilian Typhlonectes natans, the m. levator arcus branchiales complex is a triangular structure that originates from the otic capsule and dorsal trunk muscle fascia and inserts ventrally on the posteriormost ceratobranchial.
source: Based on our examination, the m. levator arcus branchiales complex is a triangular structure that originates from the otic capsule and dorsal trunk muscle fascia and inserts ventrally on the the posteriormost ceratobranchial (Figure 1E,I).
evidence: Based on CT imaging data

claim: The pars posterosuperficialis of the m. levator arcus branchialis complex in caecilians inserts on the fascia separating the rectus abdominus from the interhyoideus.
source: A posterior division of the muscle, the pars posterosuperficialis (Wilkinson and Nussbaum, 1997), inserts on the fascia separating the rectus abdominus from the interhyoideus.
evidence: Based on CT imaging data and citation to Wilkinson and Nussbaum, 1997

claim: The posterior division of the m. levator arcus branchialis complex in caecilians is homologous with the cucullaris.
source: Based on these topographic relationships, we homologize the posterior division of the m. levator arcus branchialis complex with the cucullaris.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical observations

claim: The cucullaris and its homologs comprise a highly conserved connection between head and trunk.
source: The cucullaris and its homologs comprise a highly conserved connection between head and trunk.
evidence: Inference based on comparative anatomical data across taxa

claim: The cucullaris is intimately associated, and sometimes partially continuous, with the gill levators.
source: In general, the cucullaris is intimately associated, and sometimes partially continuous, with the gill levators.
evidence: Based on CT imaging observations across taxa

claim: In numerous taxa, the cucullaris attaches to the skull and gill skeleton, both cranial elements.
source: In numerous taxa, it attaches to the skull and gill skeleton, both cranial elements.
evidence: Based on CT imaging observations

claim: In juvenile axolotls, the cucullaris resembles the condition in bichir; it is morphologically similar to and in series with the anterior gill levators.
source: In juvenile axolotls, the cucullaris resembles the condition in bichir; it is morphologically similar to and in series with the anterior gill levators, whereas in adults it expands into a broad, thin sheet (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Based on OPT and CT imaging data

claim: In adult axolotls, the cucullaris expands into a broad, thin sheet.
source: In juvenile axolotls, the cucullaris resembles the condition in bichir; it is morphologically similar to and in series with the anterior gill levators, whereas in adults it expands into a broad, thin sheet (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Based on CT imaging data

claim: In chicken and axolotl, mesoderm from somites 1 and 2 contributes to the cucullaris.
source: In chicken and axolotl, mesoderm from somites 1 and 2 contributes to the cucullaris (Piekarski and Olsson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piekarski and Olsson, 2007

claim: In chicken, the majority of the cucullaris is derived from lateral plate mesoderm adjacent to the occipital somites.
source: In chicken, however, the majority of the cucullaris is derived from lateral plate mesoderm adjacent to the occipital somites (Theis et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Theis et al., 2010

claim: Unsegmented mesoderm lateral to somites 1−3 in axolotl contributes to the levator arcuum branchiarum anlagen dorsal to the developing gills.
source: (D−F) Labeling of the levator arcuum branchiarum anlagen (laba) dorsal to the developing gills is visible in lateral (D, E) and dorsal (F) views.
evidence: Based on fate-mapping experiments with GFP labeling

claim: Unsegmented mesoderm lateral to somites 1−3 in axolotl contributes to gill-levator muscles, the cucullaris, and the dilatator laryngis.
source: (G) Gill-levator muscles (levator arcuum branchiarum, lab) of arches 3 and 4, the cucullaris (cuc) and the dilatator laryngis (dil) are labeled in a juvenile axolotl.
evidence: Based on fate-mapping experiments with GFP labeling

claim: GFP labeling following stage-21 transplantation of unsegmented mesoderm is absent from the somitic hypobranchial or epaxial muscles.
source: In cross section, labeled cells were present throughout the length of the cucullaris but absent from the somitic hypobranchial or epaxial muscles, thus indicating little if any somitic contamination (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Based on fate-mapping experiments with GFP labeling and histological analysis

claim: In most transplants of anterior cranial mesoderm in axolotl, the first gill-levator muscle originated from mesoderm just anterior to the first somite.
source: In most of these transplants, the first gill-levator muscle originated from mesoderm just anterior to the first somite, whereas the posterior three gill levators arose from unsegmented mesoderm at the level of somites 1−3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on fate-mapping experiments

claim: The posterior three gill levators in axolotl arose from unsegmented mesoderm at the level of somites 1−3.
source: In most of these transplants, the first gill-levator muscle originated from mesoderm just anterior to the first somite, whereas the posterior three gill levators arose from unsegmented mesoderm at the level of somites 1−3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on fate-mapping experiments

claim: At neurula and tailbud stages, isl1 is expressed in anterior cranial mesoderm associated with the second heart field in axolotl.
source: At neurula and tailbud stages, isl1 is expressed in anterior cranial mesoderm associated with the second heart field (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Sefton et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data and citation to Sefton et al., 2015

claim: In subsequent stages, isl1 expression expands dorsally to encompass the entire dorsoventral length of the gills in axolotl.
source: In subsequent stages, isl1 expression expands dorsally to encompass the entire dorsoventral length of the gills (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: At stage 34, isl1 expression is reduced near the heart and appears in the developing cranial placodes in axolotl.
source: In subsequent stages, isl1 expression expands dorsally to encompass the entire dorsoventral length of the gills (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), but later (stage 34) it is reduced near the heart and appears in the developing cranial placodes (Figure 2J).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: From stage 36 through at least stage 40, stripes of isl1 expression are present dorsal to the developing gills, including the levator anlage in axolotl.
source: From stage 36 through at least stage 40, stripes of expression are present dorsal to the developing gills, including the levator anlage (Figure 2K−M').
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: The cranial-mesoderm marker tbx1 is expressed in the developing gill muscle region at stages 35 and 38 in axolotl.
source: The cranial-mesoderm marker tbx1 (sequences of tbx1, msc and pitx2 by pers. comm. from J. Whited, B. Haas and L. Peshkin) is expressed in the developing gill muscle region at stages 35 and 38 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: By stage 38, msc is expressed in the gill region in axolotl.
source: By stage 38, msc is also expressed in the gill region.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: Unlike isl1, expression of tbx1 and msc extends distally into the external gills in axolotl.
source: Unlike isl1, expression of tbx1 and msc extends distally into the external gills (Figure 2—figure supplement 2O).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: Jaw adductor muscles in axolotl include the levator mandibulae externus (lme) and the levator mandibulae anterior (lma).
source: In axolotl, jaw adductor muscles include the levator mandibulae externus (lme) and the levator mandibulae anterior (lma); the latter muscle is also called the pseudotemporalis (Ziermann and Diogo, 2013).
evidence: Based on anatomical knowledge and citation to Ziermann and Diogo, 2013

claim: Both levator mandibulae externus and levator mandibulae anterior develop within the mandibular arch in axolotl.
source: Both of these muscles develop within the mandibular arch (Figure 3B,I).
evidence: Based on fate-mapping data

claim: lhx2 is expressed in the brain and eye in axolotl, as seen in mouse and Xenopus.
source: As seen in mouse and Xenopus, lhx2 is expressed in axolotl in the brain and eye (Figure 3; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A−E; Viczian et al., 2006; Atkinson-Leadbeater et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data and citations to studies in other species

claim: At stage 34, lhx2 is expressed in the mesodermal core of the pharyngeal arches in axolotl.
source: At stage 34, lhx2 is expressed in the mesodermal core of the pharyngeal arches (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: By stage 40, lhx2 expression becomes more restricted to specific muscle groups, including the lme and ventral hyoid arch musculature in axolotl.
source: but by stage 40 it becomes more restricted to specific muscle groups, including the lme and ventral hyoid arch musculature, but expression was not visible in the lma at stage 40 (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: lhx2 expression was not visible in the lma at stage 40 in axolotl.
source: but by stage 40 it becomes more restricted to specific muscle groups, including the lme and ventral hyoid arch musculature, but expression was not visible in the lma at stage 40 (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: At stage 38, the anlage of the lma is located posterior to the eye in axolotl.
source: At stage 38, the anlage of the lma is located posterior to the eye (Figure 3I).
evidence: Based on fate-mapping data

claim: By stage 40, the region forming the lma expresses isl1, including the superficial lma and developing ganglia in axolotl.
source: By stage 40, this region expresses isl1, including the superficial lma and developing ganglia, while isl1 expression was not visible in the lme (Figure 3J−K'').
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: isl1 expression was not visible in the lme at stage 40 in axolotl.
source: By stage 40, this region expresses isl1, including the superficial lma and developing ganglia, while isl1 expression was not visible in the lme (Figure 3J−K'').
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: In mouse, Pitx2 is broadly expressed in developing muscle and is required to specify mesoderm of the mandibular arch but not of the hyoid arch.
source: In mouse, Pitx2 is broadly expressed in developing muscle; it is required to specify mesoderm of the mandibular arch but not of the hyoid arch (Shih et al., 2007a; 2007b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shih et al., 2007a and 2007b

claim: In axolotl, as in chick, pitx2 is expressed in anterior ectoderm and oral region from neurula stages through at least tailbud stages.
source: In axolotl, as in chick, pitx2 is expressed in anterior ectoderm and oral region from neurula stages through at least tailbud stages (Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F−M; Bothe and Dietrich, 2006).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data and citation to Bothe and Dietrich, 2006

claim: A stripe of pitx2 expression in hyoid arch mesoderm and in the migrating hypobranchial muscle precursors appears by stage 34 in axolotl.
source: A stripe of expression in hyoid arch mesoderm and in the migrating hypobranchial muscle precursors also appears by stage 34 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: pitx2 expression is maintained in hyoid arch derivatives and by stage 40 is concentrated in the hyoid musculature, including the depressor mandibulae and branchiohyoideus externus in axolotl.
source: It is maintained in hyoid arch derivatives and by stage 40 is concentrated in the hyoid musculature, including the depressor mandibulae and branchiohyoideus externus (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1K,M).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: At stage 40, pitx2 is not expressed in gill musculature in axolotl.
source: At stage 40, pitx2 is not expressed in gill musculature, although it is strongly expressed in tongue musculature (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L,M).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: At stage 40, pitx2 is strongly expressed in tongue musculature in axolotl.
source: At stage 40, pitx2 is not expressed in gill musculature, although it is strongly expressed in tongue musculature (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L,M).
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: Myogenic lateral plate mesoderm in the cucullaris region adjacent to somite 2 was transplanted into anterior cranial mesoderm and incorporated into both dorsal and ventral mandibular arch or hyoid arch muscle.
source: Myogenic lateral plate mesoderm in the cucullaris region adjacent to somite 2 was transplanted into anterior cranial mesoderm following extirpation of a region of host mesoderm (Figure 5A). Transplanted cells were incorporated into both dorsal and ventral mandibular arch or hyoid arch muscle (Figure 5B,C'').
evidence: Based on heterotopic transplantation experiments

claim: Muscles formed from transplanted lateral plate mesoderm displayed normal innervation from the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve and the facial nerve.
source: These muscles displayed normal innervation from the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (Figure 5C−C'') and the facial nerve, respectively.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry showing nerve labeling

claim: Local cues appear sufficient to pattern myogenic lateral plate mesoderm from the cucullaris region and to promote mandibular or hyoid arch muscle development.
source: Local cues appear sufficient to pattern myogenic lateral plate mesoderm from the cucullaris region and to promote mandibular or hyoid arch muscle development.
evidence: Inference based on heterotopic transplantation experiments

claim: When more posterior lateral plate mesoderm, adjacent to somite 5, was transplanted heterotopically to mandibular arch mesoderm, in 9 of 10 larvae transplanted cells did not incorporate into muscle.
source: Next, more posterior lateral plate mesoderm, adjacent to somite 5, was transplanted heterotopically to mandibular arch mesoderm at stage 21 (Figure 5D). While transplanted cells were present among mandibular arch structures, in 9 of 10 larvae they did not incorporate into muscle (Figure 5E).
evidence: Based on heterotopic transplantation experiments

claim: Neither mandibular nor hyoid arch mesoderm appears sufficient to induce posterior non-myogenic lateral plate mesoderm to form muscle.
source: Neither mandibular nor hyoid arch mesoderm appears sufficient to induce posterior non-myogenic lateral plate mesoderm to form muscle.
evidence: Inference based on heterotopic transplantation experiments

claim: The cucullaris is a branchiomeric muscle in series with the gill levators.
source: We provide evidence from comparative morphology, embryonic fate mapping and gene expression that the cucullaris is a branchiomeric muscle in series with the gill levators and that it is stably conserved across gnathostomes as a link between head and trunk.
evidence: Based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript

claim: The cucullaris is stably conserved across gnathostomes as a link between head and trunk.
source: We provide evidence from comparative morphology, embryonic fate mapping and gene expression that the cucullaris is a branchiomeric muscle in series with the gill levators and that it is stably conserved across gnathostomes as a link between head and trunk.
evidence: Based on comparative morphological data across taxa

claim: The fifth gill levator of the coelacanth is homologous to the cucullaris.
source: Accordingly, we propose the fifth gill levator of the coelacanth to be homologous to the cucullaris, which, as in some sharks, rays and lungfish, attaches the pectoral girdle to the posteriormost gill bar (Edgeworth, 1935; Greenwood and Lauder, 1981).
evidence: Based on anatomical observations from imaging data and comparative anatomy

claim: In larval Ichthyophis kohtaoensis, a caecilian, the fourth gill levator is substantially larger than the anterior three levators.
source: In larval Ichthyophis kohtaoensis, a caecilian, the fourth gill levator is substantially larger than the anterior three levators (Kleinteich and Haas, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kleinteich and Haas, 2007

claim: The cucullaris could potentially develop from the caudalmost gill levator, as has been suggested in urodeles.
source: The cucullaris could potentially develop from the caudalmost gill levator, as has been suggested in urodeles (Edgeworth, 1935; Ziermann and Diogo, 2013).
evidence: Speculation based on citations to previous suggestions

claim: The cucullaris has evolved to perform distinct functions in different lineages.
source: The cucullaris has evolved to perform distinct functions in different lineages.
evidence: General statement based on comparative anatomy

claim: In placoderms, the cucullaris may have depressed the head.
source: In placoderms, for example, it may have depressed the head (Trinajstic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trinajstic et al., 2013

claim: The morphology of the cucullaris in sharks and rays suggests the muscle in gnathostomes originates ancestrally from the pectoral girdle and inserts on two parts of the cranial skeleton: the posterior gill bar and the caudal region of the head.
source: The morphology of the cucullaris in sharks and rays suggests the muscle in gnathostomes originates ancestrally from the pectoral girdle and inserts on two parts of the cranial skeleton: the posterior gill bar and the caudal region of the head.
evidence: Inference based on comparative anatomical observations

claim: The connection of the cucullaris to the gill arches was likely lost in early tetrapods.
source: The connection to the gill arches was likely lost in early tetrapods (but possibly later reappeared in caecilians)
evidence: Inference based on comparative anatomy

claim: An alternate attachment of the cucullaris to the clavicle evolved in some lineages.
source: while an alternate attachment to the clavicle evolved in some lineages.
evidence: Inference based on comparative anatomy

claim: Recent work suggests that the cucullaris may be present in both turtles and snakes.
source: The cucullaris is purportedly absent in turtles and snakes, but recent work suggests that it may be present in both groups.
evidence: Reference to recent literature

claim: In turtles, it has been proposed that the cucullaris originates on the shell (carapace), which incorporates parts of the pectoral girdle.
source: In turtles, it has been proposed that the muscle originates on the shell (carapace), which incorporates parts of the pectoral girdle (Lyson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lyson et al., 2013

claim: In snakes, the pectoral girdle is absent and the origin of the cucullaris has concomitantly shifted to the body wall.
source: In snakes, the pectoral girdle is absent and the origin of the cucullaris has concomitantly shifted to the body wall (Tsuihiji et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsuihiji et al., 2006

claim: In the axolotl, the cucullaris has a dual embryonic derivation from both somitic and cranial mesoderm.
source: The cucullaris is located in a complex transition zone between head and trunk; in the axolotl, this complexity is reflected in the muscle's dual embryonic derivation from both somitic and cranial mesoderm.
evidence: Based on fate-mapping data presented in the manuscript

claim: An origin of the cucullaris from both the caudal branchial levator and somites was suggested in the spotted salamander, Ambystoma maculatum, based on serial sections and dissection.
source: An origin from both the caudal branchial levator and somites was suggested in the spotted salamander, Ambystoma maculatum, based on serial sections and dissection (Piatt, 1938).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piatt, 1938

claim: Unsegmented mesoderm adjacent to the anterior somites forms the posterior gill-levator muscles, a laryngeal muscle, the levatores et depressores branchiarum and the cucullaris in axolotl.
source: Our finding that unsegmented mesoderm adjacent to the anterior somites forms the posterior gill-levator muscles, a laryngeal muscle, the levatores et depressores branchiarum and the cucullaris indicates that the posterior limit of cranial mesoderm is at somite 3.
evidence: Based on fate-mapping data

claim: The posterior limit of cranial mesoderm in axolotl is at somite 3.
source: Our finding that unsegmented mesoderm adjacent to the anterior somites forms the posterior gill-levator muscles, a laryngeal muscle, the levatores et depressores branchiarum and the cucullaris indicates that the posterior limit of cranial mesoderm is at somite 3.
evidence: Inference based on fate-mapping data

claim: The presence of labeled cranial mesoderm cells in a laryngeal muscle in axolotl betrays the deep phylogenetic conservation of a relationship between the cucullaris and laryngeal muscles.
source: The presence of labeled cranial mesoderm cells in a laryngeal muscle in axolotl betrays the deep phylogenetic conservation of a relationship between the cucullaris and laryngeal muscles, which was revealed in a recent analysis demonstrating that mouse laryngeal muscles are clonally related to the trapezius and absent following mutation of the gene Tbx1 (Lescroart et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on fate-mapping data and citation to Lescroart et al., 2015

claim: Mouse laryngeal muscles are clonally related to the trapezius and absent following mutation of the gene Tbx1.
source: which was revealed in a recent analysis demonstrating that mouse laryngeal muscles are clonally related to the trapezius and absent following mutation of the gene Tbx1 (Lescroart et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lescroart et al., 2015

claim: Expression of the genes isl1 and tbx1 in the gill-levator region suggests these muscles develop through the cranial muscle regulatory network.
source: Moreover, expression of the genes isl1 and tbx1 in the gill-levator region suggests these muscles develop through the cranial muscle regulatory network, consistent with their classical anatomical classification as cranial muscles.
evidence: Inference based on gene expression data

claim: Analysis of cranial mesoderm markers in axolotl provides additional evidence for genetic heterogeneity in cranial muscle development in anamniotes.
source: Our analysis of cranial mesoderm markers in axolotl provides additional evidence for genetic heterogeneity in cranial muscle development in anamniotes, which has been demonstrated in mouse and chicken (Nathan et al., 2008; Dong et al., 2006; Kelly et al., 2004; Marcucio and Noden, 1999).
evidence: Based on gene expression data and citations to studies in other species

claim: Differentiation of mandibular adductor muscles is present in amphibians at the level of gene expression.
source: Surprisingly, our data reveal that differentiation of mandibular adductor muscles is present in amphibians at the level of gene expression.
evidence: Based on gene expression data showing differential expression of lhx2 and isl1

claim: At stage 40, isl1 is expressed in the superficial anterior adductor in axolotl.
source: At stage 40, isl1 is expressed in the superficial anterior adductor, while lhx2 is expressed in the external adductor.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: At stage 40, lhx2 is expressed in the external adductor in axolotl.
source: At stage 40, isl1 is expressed in the superficial anterior adductor, while lhx2 is expressed in the external adductor.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data

claim: In mouse, the LIM homeodomain gene Isl1 is required for normal second heart field (SHF) development.
source: In mouse, the LIM homeodomain gene Isl1 is required for normal second heart field (SHF) development and its expression in SHF progenitors is downregulated following differentiation (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2003

claim: Genetic fate mapping in mouse demonstrates a large contribution of Isl1-positive cells to the ventral intermandibular muscle and the cucullaris.
source: Genetic fate mapping in mouse demonstrates a large contribution of Isl1-positive cells to the ventral intermandibular muscle and the cucullaris (Nathan et al., 2008; Theis et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nathan et al., 2008 and Theis et al., 2010

claim: Regionalization of developmental programs underlies cranial muscle formation, both among pharyngeal arches and even within the mandibular adductor complex.
source: Taken together, these findings underscore the regionalization of developmental programs that underlies cranial muscle formation, both among pharyngeal arches and even within the mandibular adductor complex.
evidence: Inference based on gene expression data

claim: Regionalization of developmental programs in cranial muscle formation may be an ancestral feature of tetrapod vertebrates that is retained in living taxa.
source: Moreover, the broad phylogenetic diversity of the model species involved suggests that such regionalization may be an ancestral feature of tetrapod vertebrates that is retained in living taxa and may also exist in their piscine outgroups.
evidence: Inference based on comparative data across species

claim: In the axolotl embryo, somites and pharyngeal arches are located at the same post-otic axial level.
source: In the axolotl embryo, somites and pharyngeal arches are located at the same post-otic axial level, which is a basic feature of morphologically conservative vertebrates (Kuratani, 1997).
evidence: Anatomical observation supported by citation to Kuratani, 1997

claim: Lateral plate mesoderm adjacent to somites 1 and 2 is located in the intermediate region between head and trunk and is important for morphogenetic movements associated with the migration of hypobranchial muscle progenitors.
source: Lateral plate mesoderm adjacent to somites 1 and 2 is located in the intermediate region between head and trunk and is important for morphogenetic movements associated with the migration of hypobranchial muscle progenitors (Lours-Calet et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lours-Calet et al., 2014

claim: Lengthening of the amniote neck is associated with the caudal shift of the heart into the thorax.
source: Moreover, lengthening of the amniote neck is associated with the caudal shift of the heart into the thorax (Hirasawa et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirasawa et al., 2016

claim: The head-trunk interface at the paraxial level is marked by the path of circumpharyngeal neural crest cells as they migrate ventral to the occipital somites to form the circumpharyngeal ridge caudal to the pharynx.
source: The head-trunk interface at the paraxial level is marked by the path of circumpharyngeal neural crest cells as they migrate ventral to the occipital somites to form the circumpharyngeal ridge caudal to the pharynx (Kuratani, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuratani, 1997

claim: Lateral plate mesoderm in the embryonic 'trunk' in chicken has myogenic capacity.
source: Our finding that the posterior gill-levator muscles and the cucullaris originate from cranial mesoderm adjacent to the first three somites supports categorization of the cucullaris as a branchiomeric muscle. Moreover, it may help explain why lateral plate mesoderm in the embryonic 'trunk' in chicken has myogenic capacity.
evidence: Inference based on fate-mapping data and comparison with chicken

claim: Mesoderm that gives rise to the cucullaris in amniotes is not a novel source of musculature, but instead is cranial mesoderm associated with the most posterior pharyngeal arch.
source: Our fate-mapping data suggest that this mesoderm, which gives rise to the cucullaris in amniotes, is not a novel source of musculature, but instead is cranial mesoderm associated with the most posterior pharyngeal arch (5th, 6th or 7th, depending on species).
evidence: Inference based on fate-mapping data

claim: In the axolotl, somite 3 is the posterior limit of mesodermal contribution to cranial structures in both paraxial and lateral mesoderm.
source: We propose that, in the axolotl, somite 3 is the posterior limit of mesodermal contribution to cranial structures in both paraxial and lateral mesoderm (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on fate-mapping data

claim: In heterotopic transplantations, cranial mesoderm that forms the cucullaris is able to follow the myogenic program of cranial muscles in the mandibular and hyoid arches.
source: In our heterotopic transplantations, cranial mesoderm that forms the cucullaris is able to follow the myogenic program of cranial muscles in the mandibular and hyoid arches.
evidence: Based on heterotopic transplantation experiments

claim: The chicken retains cucullaris progenitors in the same anatomical position as in the axolotl.
source: Although the chicken lacks many of the cartilages and muscles associated with the posterior pharyngeal arches in other tetrapods, it retains cucullaris progenitors in the same anatomical position as in the axolotl (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inference based on comparative anatomy and literature

claim: In the chicken, the head-trunk boundary in somites is posterior to that in unsegmented cranial mesoderm.
source: The head-trunk boundary in the axolotl is congruent between cranial mesoderm and somitic mesoderm, but in the chicken (and probably other amniotes) the head-trunk boundary in somites is posterior to that in unsegmented cranial mesoderm (Figure 6A–B; Couly et al., 1993; Piekarski and Olsson, 2014; Huang et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on comparison with literature and fate-mapping data

claim: It remains to be determined whether the congruence of the head-trunk boundary between somites and unsegmented mesoderm, as seen in the axolotl, is the plesiomorphic condition for tetrapods.
source: It remains to be determined whether this congruence, as seen in the axolotl, is the plesiomorphic condition for tetrapods.
evidence: Statement of uncertainty about evolutionary interpretation

claim: Heterotopic transplantations in chicken suggest that somitic mesoderm has greater regional plasticity than lateral plate mesoderm.
source: Heterotopic transplantations in chicken suggest that somitic mesoderm has greater regional plasticity than lateral plate mesoderm.
evidence: Reference to transplantation experiments in chicken

claim: Somites that contribute to the posterior skull in chicken are able to generate vertebrae when transplanted to a more posterior position, independent of Hox gene expression.
source: Somites that contribute to the posterior skull are able to generate vertebrae when transplanted to a more posterior position, independent of Hox gene expression (Kant and Goldstein, 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kant and Goldstein, 1999

claim: Caudal cranial mesoderm that gives rise to the cucullaris in chicken is unable to generate muscle when transplanted to a more posterior location.
source: whereas caudal cranial mesoderm that gives rise to the cucullaris is unable to generate muscle when transplanted to a more posterior location (Theis et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Theis et al., 2010
